extracted.intended_audience: U.S. patent applicants, patent attorneys/agents, and patent examiners
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and mandatory form/content standards for preparing and examining parts of a U.S. patent application specification (abstract, background, summary, drawings, detailed description, best mode, and claims). Focused on compliance with 37 CFR and MPEP practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract — length and general form
rubrics_metrics.description: The abstract should be in narrative form and generally limited to a single paragraph within the range of 50 to 150 words. The abstract should not exceed 15 lines of text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the abstract exceeds 150 words it may not fit the computer tape/printer space and the application may be returned for a shorter abstract. Avoid claim-like legal phraseology such as “means” and “said.” The abstract should sufficiently describe the disclosure to assist readers in deciding whether to consult the full patent text. Avoid repeating the title and avoid phrases which can be implied (e.g., “This disclosure concerns,” “The disclosure describes”). See MPEP § 608.01(b).

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract — substantive content (what to include)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent abstract is a concise statement of the technical disclosure of the patent and should include that which is new in the art to which the invention pertains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the patent is basic in nature, the abstract may be directed to the entire disclosure; if an improvement, the abstract should include the technical disclosure of the improvement. For compounds/compositions where process for making or use is non-obvious, the abstract should set forth a process for making and/or a use. The abstract should not refer to purported merits or speculative applications or compare the invention with the prior art. Where applicable, the abstract should include: (1) machine/apparatus organization and operation; (2) article method of making; (3) chemical compound identity and use; (4) mixture ingredients; (5) process steps. Extensive mechanical/design details should not be included. (See MPEP § 608.01(c) and form paragraph 6.14.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract — chemical case guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: In chemical patent abstracts for compounds or compositions, the general nature of the compound or composition should be given as well as its use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exemplification of a species may illustrate members of the class. For processes, state the type reaction, reagents and process conditions, generally illustrated by a single example unless variations are necessary. Complete revision of the abstract content is required on a separate sheet for such cases. (See ¶ 6.15.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract — language and prohibited phrasing
rubrics_metrics.description: The abstract should be clear and concise, avoid legal phraseology commonly used in claims, and should not repeat information given in the title.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid use of words/phrases that can be implied (e.g., “The disclosure concerns,” etc.). Avoid claim words like “means” and “said.” The abstract should describe the disclosure sufficiently to help readers judge whether to consult the full patent. (See ¶ 6.16 and Examiner Note references to form paragraph 6.14.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract — placement on separate sheet
rubrics_metrics.description: The abstract of the disclosure must commence on a separate sheet in accordance with 37 CFR 1.52(b)(4).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A new abstract on a separate sheet is required when the abstract does not commence on a separate sheet. This requirement applies to initial filings and amendments. Do not use certain form paragraphs during national stage prosecution if an abstract was published under PCT Article 21. (See ¶ 6.16.01 and related Examiner Notes.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Responsibility for abstract preparation and review
rubrics_metrics.description: Preparation of the abstract is the responsibility of the applicant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicant’s background knowledge of the art and appreciation of their contribution are important. The examiner reviews the abstract for compliance with guidelines and is responsible for necessary editing and revision on allowance of the application. For pro se applicants consider form paragraphs 6.14–6.16. (See section D.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Background of the Invention — required parts
rubrics_metrics.description: The Background of the Invention ordinarily comprises two parts: (1) Field of the Invention; and (2) Description of the related art including information disclosed under 37 CFR 1.97 and 1.98.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Field of the Invention: statement of the field of art directed to the subject matter of the claimed invention and may paraphrase U.S. patent classification definitions. Description of related art: describe the state of the prior art or other known information, include references where appropriate, and indicate problems in the prior art which are solved by the applicant’s invention. (See MPEP § 608.01(c).)

rubrics_metrics.name: Brief Summary of the Invention — content and tone
rubrics_metrics.description: A brief summary of the invention indicating its nature and substance, which may include a statement of the object of the invention, should precede the detailed description and be commensurate with the invention as claimed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The summary should be directed to the specific invention being claimed, not generalities that apply to many patents. It should describe the exact nature, operation, and purpose in clear, concise sentences or paragraphs, and be consistent with the subject matter of the claims. Stereotyped general statements may be canceled as surplusage. The brief summary aids public understanding and future searches. (See 37 CFR 1.73 and MPEP § 608.01(d).)

rubrics_metrics.name: Reservation clauses not permitted
rubrics_metrics.description: A reservation for a future application of subject matter disclosed but not claimed in a pending application will not be permitted in the pending application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An application disclosing unclaimed subject matter may reference a later filed application of the same applicant or common assignee, but cannot reserve subject matter for future claim. (See 37 CFR 1.79 and MPEP § 608.01(e).)

rubrics_metrics.name: Brief description of drawings — required content and cross-references
rubrics_metrics.description: When there are drawings, there shall be a brief description of the several views of the drawings and the detailed description shall refer to the different views by specifying figure numbers and to parts by reference letters or numerals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Office of Patent Application Processing (OPAP) will review that all figures described are present; if the specification describes a figure not present, the application may be treated as filed without all figures. Examiner should ensure figures are correctly described, all section lines are referred to, and needed section lines are used. If drawings show Figures 1A, 1B, 1C but brief description refers only to Figure 1, object and require correction. (See MPEP § 608.01(f).)

rubrics_metrics.name: Drawings — acceptable media and color drawing petition requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two acceptable categories for drawings in utility and design patent applications: (1) black ink (India ink or equivalent solid black lines) and (2) color (only in rare cases and subject to conditions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Color drawings accepted only when necessary as the only practical medium; must be reproducible in black and white in the printed patent; color drawings are not permitted in international applications or in an application submitted under the electronic filing system. Acceptance of color drawings requires a petition including the fee in § 1.17(h), submission of three sets of color drawings, and an amendment to the specification inserting specified language in the brief description of drawings. (See 37 CFR 1.84(a).)

rubrics_metrics.name: Photographs — when acceptable and quality standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Photographs (including photocopies) are not ordinarily permitted but will be accepted if photographs are the only practicable medium for illustrating the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acceptable examples include electrophoresis gels, blots, cell cultures, histological sections, animals, plants, in vivo imaging, TLC plates, crystalline structures, and ornamental effects in design patents. Examiner may require a drawing if the subject admits illustration by a drawing. Photographs must be of sufficient quality that all details are reproducible in the printed patent. Color photographs follow color-drawing conditions. (See 37 CFR 1.84(b).)

rubrics_metrics.name: Detailed description — enablement requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The detailed description, required by 37 CFR 1.71, must be in such particularity as to enable any person skilled in the pertinent art or science to make and use the invention without involving extensive experimentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicant may use their own terminology if understandable. Examiners may require necessary grammatical corrections but examination is not for grammatical perfection. See MPEP § 608.01(g) and 35 U.S.C. 112/37 CFR 1.71 references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference characters and illustrations — proper application and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Reference characters must be properly applied; no single reference character should be used for two different parts or for a part and its modification. Every feature specified in the claims must be illustrated, but there should be no superfluous illustrations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See 37 CFR 1.84(p). Improper use of reference characters (e.g., not enclosed in parentheses in claims) can be objected to (form paragraph 7.29.02). Reference characters in claims should be enclosed within parentheses to avoid confusion and are considered to have no effect on claim scope. (See MPEP § 608.01(g) and related form paragraphs.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Description must provide support/antecedent basis for claim terms
rubrics_metrics.description: The description is a dictionary for the claims and should provide clear support or antecedent basis for all terms used in the claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Terms and phrases used in claims must find clear support or antecedent basis in the description so the meaning of terms in the claims may be ascertainable by reference to the description. See 37 CFR 1.75(d)(1) and related MPEP sections (§ 608.01(i), § 608.01(o), § 1302.01).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of the Phi symbol — printing practice and consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: When the symbol Ø (slashed zero) is used by the applicant, the Office of Patent Publication will print the symbol Ø whenever that symbol is used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because many typewriters lack Greek Phi characters and applicants use various approximations, editorial staff will resolve ambiguity by printing Ø. Any Certificate of Correction necessitated by this practice will be at the patentee’s expense (37 CFR 1.323) because the intended symbol was not accurately presented. (Discussion and case citation provided.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Best mode requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The best mode contemplated by the inventor of carrying out his or her invention must be set forth in the description (35 U.S.C. 112).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is no statutory requirement for disclosure of a specific example; absence of a working example is not necessarily evidence that the best mode was not disclosed. Inadequacy is only shown by evidence of concealment such that disclosure quality effectively results in concealment. An attempt to amend to add best mode after filing should be treated as new matter and not be used to cure a failure present at filing. See cited case law and MPEP § 608.01(h) and § 2165 et seq.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims — statutory requirement and general function
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must conclude with a claim particularly pointing out and distinctly claiming the subject matter which the applicant regards as his invention or discovery (35 U.S.C. 112).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims define the protection sought and are an important part of the application. See MPEP § 608.01(i).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims — multiple/dependent claim rules and fees
rubrics_metrics.description: One or more claims may be presented provided they differ substantially and are not unduly multiplied. Dependent claims may refer back to and further limit another claim. Multiple dependent claims must refer in the alternative only and may not serve as the basis for another multiple dependent claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For fee calculation purposes a multiple dependent claim is considered to be the number of claims to which direct reference is made. Any claim depending from a multiple dependent claim is treated similarly for fee calculation. Original applications filed with or amended to include multiple dependent claims must pay the fee in § 1.16(j). See 37 CFR 1.75(c) and MPEP § 608.01(n).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims — conformity and support (meaning ascertainable)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims must conform to the invention as set forth in the remainder of the specification and the terms and phrases used in the claims must find clear support or antecedent basis in the description so that the meaning of the terms in the claims may be ascertainable by reference to the description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See 37 CFR 1.75(d)(1). Also see §§ 1.141–1.146 for claiming different inventions in one application. If the nature of the case admits (e.g., improvement), claim drafting order and phrasing guidance applies (see next rubric).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims — recommended form for improvement-type inventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Where applicable, an independent claim for an improvement should contain: (1) a preamble comprising a general description of conventional or known elements/steps; (2) a phrase such as 'wherein the improvement comprises'; and (3) those elements/steps/relationships which constitute the new or improved portion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This combination-claim form is adapted to improvement-type inventions; the preamble is considered to positively include all elements recited therein as part of the claimed combination. Use this form where the nature of the case admits. (See 37 CFR 1.75(e).)

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims — numbering, order, and placement
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims shall be numbered consecutively in Arabic numerals; the least restrictive claim should be presented as claim number 1; all dependent claims should be grouped with the claim(s) to which they refer to the extent practicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims must commence on a separate physical sheet or electronic page and may not contain any other parts of the application on that sheet. Where a claim sets forth a plurality of elements or steps, each should be separated by line indentation. The original numbering must be preserved throughout prosecution; when claims are added they must be numbered consecutively after the highest numbered claim previously presented. At allowance the examiner may renumber claims as necessary. Use form paragraphs (e.g., 6.17, 6.18.01) to notify applicant of misplacement or misnumbering. (See 37 CFR 1.126, 1.75 and related MPEP sections.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Form of claims — required formatting conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: While there is no set statutory form for claims, office practice insists each claim be the object of a sentence starting with 'I (or we) claim,' 'The invention claimed is' (or equivalent). Each claim begins with a capital letter and ends with a period; periods may not be used elsewhere in the claims except for abbreviations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where plural indentations are needed they may be used to segregate subcombinations or related steps. Reference characters may be used in claims if enclosed in parentheses and are to have no effect on claim scope. Applicants are encouraged to include claims varying from the broadest to the most detailed. Claims should be arranged in order of scope and grouped by species or product/process as appropriate to facilitate classification and examination. (See MPEP § 608.01(m).)

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims — common form objections and informalities
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims may be objected to for minor informalities such as spelling errors, inconsistent terminology, reference characters not enclosed in parentheses, or crowded line spacing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use form paragraph 7.29.01 to point out minor informalities; if the informalities render the claims indefinite use form paragraph 7.34.01 to reject under 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph. Use paragraph 7.29.02 for reference characters not enclosed in parentheses. Use paragraph 7.29.03 to object to crowded lines and require substitute claims one-and-one-half or double spaced. Amendments to claims must comply with 37 CFR 1.121(c).

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependent claims — multiple dependent claim limitations and objections
rubrics_metrics.description: A multiple dependent claim is a dependent claim which refers back in the alternative to more than one preceding independent or dependent claim; multiple dependent claims must be in alternative form, not cumulative, and may not serve as the basis for another multiple dependent claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 35 U.S.C. 112 authorizes multiple dependent claims (filed on or after Jan 24, 1978) as long as they are in alternative form (e.g., 'claims 3 or 4'). A multiple dependent claim may refer in the alternative to only one set of claims and may not serve as a basis for any other multiple dependent claim. Improper multiple dependent claims should be objected to using form paragraph 7.45, and such claims may not be further treated on the merits. Fee and counting consequences also apply as noted in multiple-dependent-claims rubric. (See MPEP § 608.01(n).)
